Trends 2015

By: Este de Klerk | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
2015 starts with high hopes - more petrol for less money... 20 year since Nelson Mandela donned the Sprinbok jersey at the Rugby WC final... What else lies in store for us?

Summary:
2015 starts with high hopes - more petrol for less money... It's also the year that marks 20 years since the legendary moment when Nelson Mandela donned the Springbok jersey at the 1995 Rugby WC final in a display of racial reconciliation.

But what lies in store for us in 2015?

Further information:
From politics to our pockets, what can we expect in 2015?

Eskom and load shedding - will it be a year of constant darkness?

E-tolls: will it be scrapped or will the Gauteng province just settle for better rates and other incentives?

President Zuma and the ANC: his popularity remains high despite his relatively poor performance in government. He will have to consolidate his power at the national general council in June. Will we see another Cabinet reshuffle? Who will succeed him - the first female President or his deputy?

Parliament: The EFF fought hard for power to be able to jump on benches and shout at chairs - no wonder the speaker didn't recognise Parliament anymore. The EFF has threatened to disrupt President Zuma's State of the Nation address on February 12. It will be the first time the President addresses the house since he left on August 21 while the EFF loudly demanded that he "pay back the money" spent on non=security upgrades at his home in Nkandla. But this year will also be a test to Parliament on how it effectively deals with the lack of decorum in the National Assembly. It has already increased the number of security personnel in the precinct.

Cosatu: Divisions and squabbles over the soul of the labour federation will reach a peak this year. At an elective conference, the factions will decide about the union's direction. At the time of Numsa's expulsion, it had the highest membership in Cosatu. Numsa has to decide whether it wants to return to the fold of the labour federation or form its own super union and workers' party.

DA opposition party: the DA has its own elective conference this year. Will leader Helen Zille hold her power or will it be challenged?

SA Economy: what will happen to the rand and the country's credit rating?

Gadgets and technology: what can we be looking forward to in terms of gadgets and new technology?

Trends: What's in and what's out - what year's fashion will we relive and what can we look forward to?

Mr. Clem Sunter Scenario planner
Mr. Stephan Grootes 702 journalist & political commentator
Mr. Goolam Ballim Economist

Mr. Dion Chang Trends Analyst

Press Release:


Trends 2015
South Africans faced a turbulent 2014 on many fronts. With the dawn of a new year, what are foremost South African economists, trend analysts and political commentators predicting for the year ahead? Carte Blanche looks into the crystal ball for telling signs on issues from the petrol price and economic growth to load shedding, e-tolling, labour union and party politics, parliamentary power plays, technology and more.


Script:


TRENDS 2015

PRODUCER: ESTé DE KLERK

BONGANI LINK: According to the Chinese calender, 2014 was the year of the Horse. It galloped past and was over before you knew it. This is the year of the Sheep, representing tranquillity and stability, but the story of 2015 is still being written.

This week, world headlines were dominated by the attack on French satirical magazine, Charlie Hebdo’s offices in Paris following its publication of cartoons perceived to ridicule the prophet Mohammed.
Gunmen left several people critically injured and at least twelve dead.

But back in South Africa, the year has started on a high…

BONGANI LINK: Thank you. News has a funny way of telling its own story. But in 2015 you can expect more of the same headlines: Eskom, load shedding, Nkandla, Julius… But for now at least, there is some good news.

On Wednesday, the petrol price dropped by more than a rand per litre. Now, South Africans who fill up a 50-litre tank once a week will save over R200 a month - bringing some financial relief to millions of over-burdened consumers, says scenario planner Clem Sunter.

CLEM SUNTER: It’s just fantastic from the point of view of inflation, particularly here in South Africa. But obviously for oil producers in the Middle East, Venezuela and Russia, it’s not good.
[ECONOMY]

BONGANI LINK: It’s the economy, Stupid. Show me the money! See, now matter how depressing our politics can get or how exciting this year’s new gadgets wil be, what most of us really want to know is what 2015 will put in our back pockets.

Government, the Reserve Bank and credit rating agencies are all hopeful that South Africa’s GDP will rise to 2,5% this year. Not an easy target, says economist, Goolam Ballim.

GOOLAM BALLIM/CHIEF ECONOMIST STANDARD BANK: It’s lower than our potential, it is poorer than emerging market peers and it is less than half the performance of the go-go years in the early 2000’s.

2014 was a turbulent year on many levels. The country lurched from one labour strike to the next – stifling the economy.

GOOLAM BALLIM: There needs to be a far more larger, more structural rejuvenation in terms of relations between labour and firms, labour and the state.

BONGANI: We heard from Finance Minister at his mid-term budget speech that we might see tax increases?

GOOLAM BALLIM: The South African government, not quite having run out of money, has hit some very hard financial ceilings and are now on a financial diet. Government’s revenue is not necessarily as buoyant in its growth as yesteryear and as a function of that they now have to rely on other methods to boy revenue.

Clem Sunter however is upbeat about the possibility that South Africa could push growth beyond 3% this year - but only if the ANC heeds certain resolutions, he says: like curtailing excessive spending and by realising that jobs can only be created by enabling new enterprises.

CLEM SUNTER: Yes, there’s been black economic empowerment. We haven’t got a generation of black entrepreneurs and industrialists to feel that we got a really representative economy. So, we got to fix it.

BONGANI: How have the electricity constraints effected our economic outlook?

GOOLAM BALLIM: The reality is that this is a constraint that is harming job creation. We estimate that we have forgone at least half of a percentage point each year in the last four years.

We were hit with rolling black-outs late last year.
And, with industry back in full swing and energy requirements rising, February and March are code red months for power cuts.
The new Medupi and Kusile power stations are meant to add 9 600MW to the stressed grid.
But, while Medupi’s first unit was expected to come into operation this week, it’s reported that it won’t be ready before Easter.

[POLITICS]

BONGANI LINK: When it comes to our politics, you could say that the year 2014 was the year of unfinished business. So, whether it was Nkandla, “Pay back the money”, or Julius Malema’s own legal woes, expect this to be the year of tying-up loose ends.

STEPHEN GROOTES/SENIOR POLITICAL CORRESPONDENT EWN: Politically, we are easily becoming more democratic. There is the prospect of more voices coming through the split-up of Cosatu, the political party – the workers party that Numsa has said it wants to create. What we are beginning to see for the first time is the ANC being challenged and that means that generally speaking it needs to become more accountable and perform better in order to stay in power. That means the ordinary voter actually has more power than they ever really had in the past.

The divisions over the soul of the labour federation, Cosatu, are set to reach a peak this year, following the expulsion of Numsa in November last year.

The ANC and its tripartite alliance partners, the SACP and what remains of Cosatu, are likely to pay a heavy price politically, financially and at the polls during next year’s municipal elections.

BONGANI: Are we likely to see Jacob Zuma’s early retirement?

STEPHEN GROOTES: The Zuma political-machine is alive and well and basically running the show. There doesn’t seem to be any serious challenge at this point and we can see this in how Ciryl Ramaphosa, the deputy President, behaves. If he thought the Zuma-machine was not running as well as it has been, he would be rocking it a little, and he’s not.

Unlike Julius Malema and the EFF who, in 2014, ushered in their brand of “ungovernable” politics.

EFF IN PARLIAMENT: Pay back the money! Pay back the money! Pay back the money!

February 12 is the opening of Parliament ánd when President Zuma will be delivering his State of the Nation Address. The EFF has threatened to disrupt it unless Zuma addresses the Nkandla issue.

STEPHEN GROOTES: It’s going to be President Jacob Zuma’s Watergate if I can call it that.

CLEM SUNTER: It has unfortunately tainted our image as a country.

STEPHEN GROOTES: The idea of the DA and the EFF working together is just madness, but on this they will work together and gives the issue such power.

In 2015, we will see disciplinary hearings and court cases around Nkandla.
But Julius Malema himself will also be in court a lot this year.

STEPHEN GROOTES: “Pay back the money”, the strong slogan for Malema now, could be used against him if it is shown that he potentially manipulated government tenders in Limpopo. I mean, he would look like the person stealing from the poor.

[TECHNOLOGY]

BONGANI LINK: When South Africa hosted the World Cup in 2010, the big toy was the Vuvuzela. Nobody had seen this or this. Yes, that’s right! Tablets weren’t on the market yet and that’s how quickly technology can change.

Most of us only think of the internet as the device allowing for communication online and quick access to information. But more devices are now connected to the internet than people - and those connections are set to reach 25 billion this year.

Good news for South Africans is that the speed of our internet connectivity will soon be superfast with the implementation of fibre.

TOBY SHAPSHAK: People still have a fear of bill-shock. A lot of South Africans use a cellular service to get the internet connection and with fibre that is going to bring the cost down.

“Wearable” technology could be the next decade’s defining advancement. From smart clothes monitoring your heart rate to smart watches. But for now, Toby says, he still enjoys his super-smart phablet.

TOBY SHAPSHAK: What is a phablet? It is in between a smart phone and a tablet and what you’ve got is something that is much more portable, it fits in your pocket, it provides a whole lot of things that you used to get on a tablet and is now the fastest growing category in mobile devices.

[TRENDS]

BONGANI TRENDS LINK: So, the selfie-stick came out late 2014, but it’s my prediction for this year’s next big thing. And that’s why I’m not a trends specialist.

But Dion Chang is, and says the selfie-stick is passé. Drones, however, are becoming a trend globally. From delivering pizzas to saving lives, the sky’s the limit for this technology.

DION CHANG/TRENDS ANALYST: There’s already something called an ambulance drone. So, if somebody falls down and you are not sure, but probably has a heart attack, you call and instead of an ambulance coming through, they will fly a drone there and it’s got a camera in it, it has regulators, it has all kind of medical kit and a medical professional talks you through the camera.

Another trend becoming more popular is egg-freezing parties: groups of women getting together to learn more about the egg-freezing process from a fertility expert.

DION CHANG: So, the egg freezing party is a manifestation of this delayed parenthood in saying: we actually want a career and through science and technology you are able to have children much, much later.

From wearables to drone-technology; phablets to fibre; how Parliament will deal with the decorum in the National Assembly, Julius Malema and the EFF; Nkandla; the ANC and President Zuma.
2015 is set to write another dramatic South African story…

Good news for South Africans is that the speed of our internet connectivity will soon be superfast with the implementation of fibre. TOBY SHAPSHAK: People still have a fear of bill-shock. A lot of South Africans use a cellular service to get the internet connection and with fibre that is going to bring the cost down. “Wearable” technology could be the next decade’s defining advancement. From smart clothes monitoring your heart rate to smart watches. But for now, Toby says, he still enjoys his super-smart phablet. TOBY SHAPSHAK: What is a phablet? It is in between a smart phone and a tablet and what you’ve got is something that is much more portable, it fits in your pocket, it provides a whole lot of things that you used to get on a tablet and is now the fastest growing category in mobile devices. [TRENDS] BONGANI TRENDS LINK: So, the selfie-stick came out late 2014, but it’s my prediction for this year’s next big thing. And that’s why I’m not a trends specialist. But Dion Chang is, and says the selfie-stick is passé. Drones, however, are becoming a trend globally. From delivering pizzas to saving lives, the sky’s the limit for this technology. DION CHANG/TRENDS ANALYST: There’s already something called an ambulance drone. So, if somebody falls down and you are not sure, but probably has a heart attack, you call and instead of an ambulance coming through, they will fly a drone there and it’s got a camera in it, it has regulators, it has all kind of medical kit and a medical professional talks you through the camera. Another trend becoming more popular is egg-freezing parties: groups of women getting together to learn more about the egg-freezing process from a fertility expert. DION CHANG: So, the egg freezing party is a manifestation of this delayed parenthood in saying: we actually want a career and through science and technology you are able to have children much, much later. From wearables to drone-technology; phablets to fibre; how Parliament will deal with the decorum in the National Assembly, Julius Malema and the EFF; Nkandla; the ANC and President Zuma. 2015 is set to write another dramatic South African story… Invoicing Back references from Insert ID in Invoice: Title Author Last Updated Invoice for Trends 2015 (4468 ) Este de Klerk 12 January 2015

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): 2015 starts with high hopes - more petrol for less money... 20 year since Nelson Mandela donned the Sprinbok jersey at the Rugby WC final... What else lies in store for us?
metadata.Summary: 2015 starts with high hopes - more petrol for less money... It's also the year that marks 20 years since the legendary moment when Nelson Mandela donned the Springbok jersey at the 1995 Rugby WC final in a display of racial reconciliation. But what lies in store for us in 2015?
metadata.Further information: From politics to our pockets, what can we expect in 2015? Eskom and load shedding - will it be a year of constant darkness? E-tolls: will it be scrapped or will the Gauteng province just settle for better rates and other incentives? President Zuma and the ANC: his popularity remains high despite his relatively poor performance in government. He will have to consolidate his power at the national general council in June. Will we see another Cabinet reshuffle? Who will succeed him - the first female President or his deputy? Parliament: The EFF fought hard for power to be able to jump on benches and shout at chairs - no wonder the speaker didn't recognise Parliament anymore. The EFF has threatened to disrupt President Zuma's State of the Nation address on February 12. It will be the first time the President addresses the house since he left on August 21 while the EFF loudly demanded that he "pay back the money" spent on non=security upgrades at his home in Nkandla. But this year will also be a test to Parliament on how it effectively deals with the lack of decorum in the National Assembly. It has already increased the number of security personnel in the precinct. Cosatu: Divisions and squabbles over the soul of the labour federation will reach a peak this year. At an elective conference, the factions will decide about the union's direction. At the time of Numsa's expulsion, it had the highest membership in Cosatu. Numsa has to decide whether it wants to return to the fold of the labour federation or form its own super union and workers' party. DA opposition party: the DA has its own elective conference this year. Will leader Helen Zille hold her power or will it be challenged? SA Economy: what will happen to the rand and the country's credit rating? Gadgets and technology: what can we be looking forward to in terms of gadgets and new technology? Trends: What's in and what's out - what year's fashion will we relive and what can we look forward to?
